title: Pulse Check Decisions
text:
What is the big picture?
Only a few things really matter

If they don’t have a pulse, someone is performing high quality compressions with NO significant breaks

Limit pauses (position changes, pulse checks, intubation, Lucas)

Shock early when they have a shockable rhythm

title: Ending the Code/RRT

That’s average, but consider:

Pre-arrest state? more ill (esp. if chronic) → shorter
Is the likely cause reversible? yes → longer
What’s the rhythm?

Asystole → bad (shorter).

title: 2026 Code Blue and Rapid Response Seminar
text:
Why This Course Exists
Code Blue and Rapid Response leadership is not just algorithm recall. The resident leader has to make the room work: claim the leader role, make roles visible, keep communication psychologically safe, and escalate resources before the response stalls.
Stakeholders from Code Blue and Rapid Response teams, including senior residents, nurses, respiratory therapists, and quality leads, identified three recurring hazards during resident-led responses:

Unclear team leadership, which can cause role confusion, low psychological safety, and decreased collaboration. (Steinbach et al. 2024)
Failure to cardiovert or defibrillate shockable rhythms.
Delayed critical decisions, including calling for help, initial stabilization, and transport to ICU.

This seminar targets those hazards through brief micro-skills, discussion, and hands-on scenarios.

title: Modules
text: These modules are the brief teaching blocks we will walk through together at the start of the session. They stay posted here for review afterward and for use during real responses.

1. Leadership Skills
Practice explicitly establishing who is leading, where to stand, and how to invite useful input from the team.
Open slides


2. Pulse-Check Decisions
Practice shock/no-shock decisions, minimizing pauses, and using EtCO2 or other signals when ROSC is uncertain.
Open slides


3. Resources and Escalation
Practice deciding whether the event is still a rapid, whether it is becoming a code, and what extra personnel or resources are needed.
Open slides


4. Ending and Debriefing
Practice ICU transfer decisions, floor handoffs, family presence, stopping an unsuccessful code, and setting a debrief.
Open slides

title: Resources
text: Quick reference materials for Code Blue and Rapid Response leadership.

title: Resources
text:
Key Points

Establish the leader early. Try: “I’m Joe/Jane Doe, the resident on the code team. Who is running this code/RRT?” or “Can I take over?”
Stay at the foot of the bed when leading. Do not drift into tasks that pull you out of room management.
Keep the big picture visible. For an RRT, ask whether this is becoming a code or whether the patient needs ICU. For a code, protect high-quality compressions and shock early if shockable.
